newsitem.title: BELGIUM: U.S. ruffles EU feathers in meat trade deal.
newsitem.headline: U.S. ruffles EU feathers in meat trade deal.

text.p: The European Commission said Friday it may take the United States to the World Trade Organisation because of Washington's plans to block imports of EU poultry in a dispute over food safety rules.
The dispute marred a deal in Washington Wednesday on mutually acceptable inspection rules covering $3 billion of trade annually in red meat, dairy, fish, egg and pet food products.

"We have to wait (and see) exactly what they (the plans) are," Commission chief spokesman Nicholas Van der Pas told a news briefing. "We do not rule out the possibility to go to the WTO because we think that such measures on the basis of the announcements would indeed be unjustified."
On Wednesday, the chief U.S. negotiator Paul Drazek said up to $1.0 million of imports of European poultry products, mainly French chicken pate, would be blocked.

The measure would come as retaliation after the EU April 1 imposed curbs on imports of $50 million of U.S. poultry, saying that the U.S. method of decontaminating chicken carcasses in chlorinated water posed a threat to consumer health.
EU poultry plants will have to be inspected to see if they comply with tough new U.S. meat inspection rules, which could take a couple of months, U.S. government sources said.
They added that Washington will not lower its standards, which are scientifically based and apply to all suppliers, to meet EU requirements.
In a statement, EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler said the agreement, after long and difficult discussions, marked an important step in boosting trade in red meat.
The agreement allows each side to accept the other's meat, dairy and fish products even though they have different inspection methods.
Fischler regretted that the United States rejected Brussels' offer of a temporary solution over poultry allowing the U.S. industry to use other chemicals to make chickens safe to eat.

Instead, the United States was planning to retaliate against EU import curbs by taking unjustified and unfair action against the EU poultry industry even though it was committed to respecting U.S. sanitary measures, he said.
"The U.S. action would be clearly in breach of its WTO sanitary and phytosanitary measures obligations, and the EC would have to consider the appropriate action to be taken," Fischler added.
Although further talks are planned, commission officials said no date had been fixed and did not foresee any early settlement.
The U.S. sources said more flexible inspection arrangements in the agreement should open new opportunies for meat exports, especially of pork, given the EU's problems with swine fever.

U.S. beef exporters hope to receive a further boost from the World Trade Organisation in Geneva next week when a disputes panel may call for the lifting of an EU ban on imports of hormone-treated beef from the United States and other suppliers.
